blocks.x: “Don’t take anything personally. Nothing others do is because of you.” ~Don Miguel Ruiz
I used to walk into a room and check everyone else’s emotional temperature before I noticed my own.

A tightened jaw meant I should get quieter. A distracted answer meant I’d done something wrong. If my partner sighed while unloading the dishwasher, I’d go back through the last hour looking for the mistake that caused it.
I called this empathy. It felt like attentiveness, and honestly, I was proud of it, because I noticed things other people missed.
What I didn’t see was that I wasn’t only noticing other people’s feelings. I was borrowing them, wrapping a story around them, and then carrying that story as evidence about myself.
The Night
One evening I texted my partner, who was staying at his sister’s place that week, and asked if he wanted to talk. The reply came four minutes later: “Can’t talk tonight”
No period. I noticed that right away, and then I analyzed the absence of it, which tells you most of what you need to know about me back then.
I read those three words until they changed shape. Maybe he was angry. Maybe I’d asked for too much lately, or maybe “tonight” was a soft way of saying “anymore.”
I typed, “Is everything okay?” and erased it because it sounded needy.
I typed, “No worries!” and erased that too, because the exclamation point looked false.
Then I carried my phone from room to room for three hours. I washed a mug that was already clean. I opened the fridge, looked at a jar of olives, and closed it again.
Every so often I checked whether he’d been online. Whatever I found, or didn’t find, I filed as evidence in a case against myself.
By eleven I had a whole theory built out of nothing. It had a timeline, a probable cause, and a list of things I planned to say once he finally admitted what was wrong.
Near midnight I sent, “Did I do something?”
The answer came the next morning. He’d had a headache, gone to bed at nine, and hadn’t been thinking about me at all.
Relief came first. Embarrassment came right behind it, hot and fast.
Underneath both was something quieter. I’d lost an entire evening to a feeling that wasn’t mine and a story nobody had told me.
His maybe-disappointment had become my panic. His silence had become my verdict.
Where I Learned It
That night wasn’t an isolated overreaction. It was a skill I’d been practicing since I was small.
As a kid, I could tell what kind of evening it would be from the sound of keys at the front door. Whether a cupboard closed or got closed. Whether a question got a full answer or a clipped one.

Nobody told me to monitor the weather in the house. I just figured out that predicting a mood gave me a few seconds to prepare for it. My brother learned to leave the room, and I learned to stay in it and read the air.
That sensitivity came with me into adulthood, where it stopped protecting me and started running me. I was treating ordinary pauses like sirens.

From the outside I probably looked easygoing. Inside I was adjusting constantly, changing the subject when someone shifted in their chair, softening an honest opinion before anyone had objected to it.
The more attention I gave to everyone else’s mood, the harder it got to locate my own. If someone was disappointed, I felt ashamed. If someone went distant, I got frantic.
This didn’t make me kinder. It made my care anxious and a little controlling.

I don’t love admitting the next part. When my partner came home flattened by a bad day that had nothing to do with me, I’d keep asking what was wrong, in a softer and softer voice, until he ended up comforting me about his own bad day.
I wanted closeness, and my monitoring was the thing standing in the way of it. I was in a relationship with my predictions instead of the person in the kitchen.
What Actually Helped
The first thing that helped was small enough to feel like nothing. I started naming the feeling before I explained it.

When a message went unanswered, I’d try, “I feel anxious,” instead of, “He’s ignoring me.” One of those describes what’s happening in my chest. The other claims to know what’s happening inside someone else’s head.
Almost all of my suffering lived in the space between those two sentences. Anxiety can be felt without being obeyed. A story about rejection demands action immediately.
I also gave myself ten minutes before sending the anxious text. No scrolling, no rereading old conversations, no drafting a fourth polite version of the same question.
The feeling in those ten minutes was usually more specific than I expected. Tight chest, warm face, a dropping sensation like missing a step on the stairs.

And when I did reach out, I tried to ask one clean question instead of a loaded one. “You seemed quiet earlier. Is something on your mind?” leaves room for an answer I hadn’t already written for them.
“Are you mad at me?” doesn’t leave that room. It hands my fear across the table and asks the other person to hold it.

That’s the line I keep coming back to now: am I asking for support or asking for proof? Support sounds like, “I’m having a tender day. Can we talk when you have a minute?” Proof sounds like, “Tell me we’re okay right now.”
Nothing anyone says to the second one lasts. The calm it buys is gone by the next delayed reply.
A few months later my closest friend left me a voice message in a flat tone I didn’t recognize, saying she’d call me back when she had a minute.
I did the ten minutes. I did them badly. I sat on the kitchen floor with the timer going and mentally rehearsed apologies for things I hadn’t done.
At minute eleven I called her anyway, and the first sentence out of my mouth was, “Are you upset with me?”
She wasn’t. Her mother had been admitted to the hospital that morning, and she’d been on the phone with doctors since six.
So the pause didn’t save me that day. What it gave me was a place to notice, halfway through my own question, that I was turning her worst week into a referendum on me.
I said that out loud. “Sorry, ignore me. Tell me about your mom.” It wasn’t a graceful recovery, but it was a different ending than the one I used to get.
Then I apologized for the phone call twice more that week, which was its own quiet way of asking her to reassure me. Some of this I’m still learning.
I still notice moods fast. I still hear the pause before an answer, still catch the smile that doesn’t quite reach someone’s eyes.
I never wanted to be less sensitive. I wanted to stop confusing sensitivity with responsibility.
Empathy means I can see that someone might be hurting. It doesn’t mean their hurt belongs to me, or was caused by me, or is mine to fix before dinner.
There are still evenings when a short message sets off the old alarm and my mind starts building explanations before I’ve taken a full breath. Some of those evenings I still lose.
More often now, though, I put the phone face down and let the feeling be mine for a while.
Sometimes there’s a real problem waiting on the other side of the screen. Usually there’s just a tired person on one end of it and my old fear on the other.
